title: Week 2 Complete — XAUUSD Cent Bot Forward Test
author: _Mann_98
selftext:
2 weeks of forward testing completed. 📊

💵 Starting balance: 49,998.48 cents (\~$500.00)

💰 Current balance: 67,508.09 cents (\~$675.08)

📈 Total profit: 17,509.61 cents (\~$175.10)

📊 Total return: +35.02%

📈 Week 2 profit: 8,913.98 cents (\~$89.14)

The account has now grown from approximately $500 → $675.08 over the first two weeks.

There was also a losing day caused by a VPS issue, which I'm including in the record rather than hiding it. The goal is to document the complete forward test, not just the profitable days.

Still a very small sample, so I'm not calling this proof of long-term profitability. The next objective is simply to keep testing through different market conditions and build a much larger track record.

comments.author: Fynca
comments.body:
Two weeks of forward testing is a good start, but the profit alone is difficult to evaluate without the starting balance, total number of trades and maximum drawdown.

I also noticed the position sizes increasing from 0.01 to 0.02 and 0.03. Does the bot use a grid or recovery strategy?

If so, the key test is what happens when gold makes a strong move without retracing. Are you tracking floating drawdown, maximum margin usage and a hard risk limit for the entire basket?

replies.author: _Mann_98
replies.body:
That's a fair question. You're right that profit alone doesn't tell the whole story.
For context, the forward test started with 49,998.48 cents (~$500) and is currently at 67,508.09 cents (~$675). I'm documenting the results day by day, and I'll be tracking the deeper metrics as the sample grows.
And yes, the increasing position sizes are part of the bot's recovery logic. I wouldn't describe it simply as a traditional grid, though—the entries and recovery conditions are rule-based.
The scenario you're mentioning is definitely one of the things I'm watching closely with XAUUSD. A strong one-directional move without a meaningful retracement is one of the most important stress cases for this type of system.
Two weeks is nowhere near enough data to claim the system is robust. That's exactly why I'm continuing the forward test instead of drawing conclusions from the current return.

replies.author: Fynca
replies.body:
That makes sense, and I appreciate the transparency. A rule-based recovery system is very different from blindly increasing position sizes, but the tail risk is still where the real test will be.

With a 35% return in two weeks, I’d define the limits now before more results come in: maximum number of recovery entries, maximum total exposure, a basket-level stop and maximum allowable floating drawdown.

I’d also track the equity curve separately from the balance curve, since closed profits can look smooth while open recovery positions are carrying significant risk.

Are you planning to publish both curves in future updates?

replies.author: _Mann_98
replies.body:
Yes, I agree. The equity curve is probably more important than the balance curve for this type of system because it shows what is happening with open positions and floating drawdown.
So far I've mainly been posting the daily closed P&L, but after your suggestion I'm going to start tracking equity alongside balance, as well as maximum floating drawdown and recovery depth.
I also agree that defining the risk limits before the sample gets much larger is important. I don't want to look at the results afterward and decide that the risk was acceptable just because the account was profitable.
I'm still working on determining the appropriate limits for the system rather than inventing numbers just to make the results look safer. The next updates should give a much better picture of the actual risk profile.
Appreciate the constructive feedback. This is exactly the kind of analysis I want to include as the forward test gets longer.

replies.author: Fynca
replies.body:
That sounds like a solid approach. I agree that the limits shouldn’t be chosen afterward simply because the returns looked good.

One distinction I’d make is that emergency account-level limits should exist before the next phase, while the growing sample can help refine the normal operational limits.

One additional metric worth tracking is time underwater, meaning the longest duration of an open recovery basket. A system can keep drawdown within its limits but still tie up capital and margin for a long time.

Recovery depth together with recovery duration should give a much clearer picture of how the system behaves under stress. Looking forward to the next update.

comments.author: tradematesHQ
comments.body: 35% in two weeks on a cent account is exactly what a martingale-style recovery bot looks like before it blows up. The fact that position sizes are increasing from 0.01 to 0.03 confirms it  -  you're averaging into losers. The VPS issue that caused a losing day is nothing compared to what happens when gold trends hard without retracing. Define your max drawdown and basket-level stop now, or this forward test ends with a $0 balance. Track the floating drawdown, not just the profit.

replies.author: _Mann_98
replies.body:
I understand the concern, and honestly this is exactly why I'm doing a live forward test rather than assuming the backtest proves anything.
You're right that increasing exposure during a recovery cycle creates a very different risk profile from a simple fixed-lot strategy. I wouldn't claim that the current return proves the system is safe.
I'm going to start tracking maximum floating drawdown, maximum recovery depth, total open exposure and margin usage, rather than looking only at closed P&L.
The important stress case is exactly what you mentioned: a strong one-directional XAUUSD move without the retracement the recovery logic expects.
I also don't want to invent an arbitrary basket stop just to make the strategy look safer. The risk limits need to be tested against the actual historical and forward-test behavior first.
So for now, I'm treating the 35% return as an observation, not a success certificate. The next stage of the test is understanding how much risk was required to generate it.
